item.title: Lawyers for Mississippi say foster care system doesn’t violate US Constitution, again ask to end federal oversight
item.dc:creator: Allen Siegler
item.description: Mississippi’s government said health and safety problems in the foster care system are not being intentionally ignored as the state’s attorneys continue their efforts to dismiss federal oversight over its child welfare system.  In a Tuesday court filing, lawyers from Mississippi’s Attorney General’s Office and the private law firm Baker Donelson said the issues that a court-appointed monitor identified in a recent report do not violate the U.S. Constitution.
item.content:encoded:
Mississippi’s government said health and safety problems in the foster care system are not being intentionally ignored as the state’s attorneys continue their efforts to dismiss federal oversight over its child welfare system. 

In a Tuesday court filing, lawyers from Mississippi’s Attorney General’s Office and the private law firm Baker Donelson said the issues that a court-appointed monitor identified in a recent report do not violate the U.S. Constitution. 

The monitoring is federally required by the 22-year-old Olivia Y. v. Barbour lawsuit — in which lawyers representing Mississippi foster children have repeatedly said the state’s child welfare efforts are systematically dangerous. 

In 2018, lawyers representing both the state and foster children in Mississippi agreed to an independent monitoring program that would annually examine over 100 safety measures. The agreement says the state government can dismiss the monitoring after it has met all the safety measures for at least a year. 

In the latest report, published in July, the independent monitor found the Mississippi Department of Child Protection Services had only met 22 of the applicable 107 measures, ranging from maltreatment in state care to placing children in unlicensed homes.

Mississippi’s lawyers questioned how the monitor went about creating the report in their Tuesday filing. They said Gov. Tate Reeves and department Commissioner Andrea Sanders have not deliberately caused these safety problems. 

The lawyers argue that Mississippi’s child welfare department has worked with the state Legislature to solve these problems and that should be enough to show the state is meeting its constitutional responsibility. 

“They have identified risks, marshaled resources, enacted legislation, rebuilt staffing, modernized technology, and restructured MDCPS to protect children’s personal security and reasonably safe living conditions,” the state’s attorneys wrote in their filing. 

Marcia Lowry, the lead lawyer representing Mississippi foster children, said Wednesday that the 2018 agreement was a legal contract, one that Mississippi’s government had not yet met the standards required to end. She said lawyers for the state knew they would be measured by the agreement rather than the Constitution when they signed onto it. 

“That’s how the case is supposed to end,” Lowry said. “It’s not supposed to end by the state now saying ‘We’ve done a bunch of different things, and we think that satisfies the constitutional standard.’” 

Lawyers for the department also said the required safety measures were “aspirational” metrics and they couldn’t be used to show Mississippi’s government wasn’t trying to address foster children’s safety. 

The 2018 agreement says the monitoring is intended to “maintain the child welfare infrastructure, standards, and outcomes that Defendants must meet within specified timeframes statewide.” Lowry said all the lawyers knew that these safety standards were enforceable when they signed the contract and the “aspirational” goals were not optional. 

“We entered into this because this is what we thought they could and should agree to get to, what they should get to over a period of time,” she said. “This is what the state agreed to.”

Clint Pentecost, the Baker Donelson lawyer who submitted the late Tuesday filing, did not answer a phone call or return a voicemail from Mississippi Today by publication time. MaryAsa Lee, spokesperson for Mississippi Attorney General Lynn Fitch, did not respond to an email.

The Olivia Y. lawsuit has lingered in the legal system for decades while Mississippi children continue to enter and exit the state’s child welfare system. Zoey Tether spent some of her teenage years in Mississippi’s foster care system, cycling through at least 10 foster care placements until the state found her a permanent home. She said at one of those placements, the adults responsible for her gave her so much medication that she could barely stay awake. 

Now 21 years old and living in Pontotoc County, she’s gotten to know other Missisisppi former foster children. She said they all have plenty of stories like hers, where they feared for their well-being as the state said it would keep them safe. 

“Where are these reasonably safe places?” Tether asked when told about the state’s filing. “One out of 10 is not reasonable.”

She said whether intentional or not, the consequences of unsafe living conditions are carried by people like her — kids who often have no choice over where they end up. For a state agency charged with those responsibilities, Tether said it’s hard for her to even think about allowing any margin of error. 

“What you miss is children and their lives,” she said.

Chief U.S. District Judge Sul Ozerden will decide what happens next in the lawsuit. Lawyers for the state asked Ozerden to either end federal foster care oversight or hold a hearing for the case, one where each side could present more evidence. Lowry said she and the other lawyers would be prepared for a hearing if Ozerden opts for one. 

Anna Hu contributed reporting to this story from Pontotoc.

item.title: 2nd man denied bond in death of Tasia Fortune, as Jackson police search for more suspects
item.dc:creator: Simeon Gates
item.description: The Jackson Police Department is asking help from the U.S. Marshals Service in arresting at least one other suspect in the death of Tasia Fortune, the 29-year-old woman found hanging from a tree last month in west Jackson. Authorities have now arrested two men in connection with the killing.
item.content:encoded:
A second man was denied bond Wednesday in connection with the killing of Tasia Fortune, a 29-year-old mother of four who was found last month hanging from a tree in west Jackson. 

Jackson Police Chief RaShall Brackney announced the arrest of Earnest Lloyd Jr., 25,  Tuesday at the Jackson City Council meeting. She said the Jackson Police Department is seeking help from the U.S. Marshals Service to arrest at least one other person. 

“I will guarantee you, there are actually more arrests to come in this incident,” Brackney said at the meeting.

Last week, police charged Jarques Ratliff, 51, with Fortune’s killing. He pleaded not guilty and remains in custody after being denied bond. His attorney said a preliminary hearing is scheduled for Friday.

Fortune’s death became national news, as the story of a Black woman found hanging harkened back to Mississippi’s dark history of racist terror lynchings. Both Lloyd and Ratliff are also Black.

On Aug. 3, Fortune’s body was found hanging from a tree outside a vacant house on the 500 block of Road of Remembrance.

Christy Spivey, Fortune’s mother, was at the meeting when the police chief announced the latest arrest. She and her husband traveled from Kentucky to be in Jackson this week to attend the court dates of the two suspects and to visit Fortune’s children. 

She held a press conference with Jackson City Councilman Kenneth Stokes before the Tuesday council meeting. Stokes is trying to schedule a meeting with the U.S. Attorney and the FBI.

“You know, she didn’t have a lot to give, she was struggling,” Spivey said at the press conference. “But she would do anything to help anybody.”

Spivey told Mississippi Today that the recent arrests, after a “brutal silence,” have given her hope that authorities are now more aggressively seeking justice for her daughter. She said the family is anxious about any additional arrests.

Spivey also visited the crime scene for the first time on Tuesday. 

“It was hard, but I felt like I owed it to Tasia,” she said.

Spivey described seeing cardinals flying, and she took pictures of her daughter’s memorial, a small mound of flowers, balloons, teddy bears and pinwheels surrounding a framed picture of her.
item.media:description: Christy Spivey poses with a portrait of her late daughter Tasia Fortune, Tuesday, Sept. 8, 2026, in Marion, Ky.

item.title: Two former Capitol Police officers go on trial on manslaughter charge
item.dc:creator: Jerry Mitchell and Claudia Amendoeira
item.description: Steven Frederick Jr. and Michael Lamar Rhinewalt, who are both white, were part of the crime suppression Flex Unit of the Capitol Police involved in the death of a Black man, Jaylen Lewis, on Sept. 25, 2022.
item.content:encoded:
The trial began Wednesday for two former Capitol Police officers charged with manslaughter in the shooting death of a 25-year-old Jackson man, with prosecutors and defense attorneys arguing over whether the shooting was in self-defense.

Steven Frederick Jr. and Michael Lamar Rhinewalt, who are both white, were part of the crime suppression Flex Unit of the Capitol Police involved in the death of a Black man, Jaylen Lewis, on Sept. 25, 2022. 

The officers stopped Lewis’ vehicle after a traffic violation and fatally shot him a few seconds later, according to testimony. Frederick, who is the son-in-law of Rankin County Sheriff Bryan Bailey, and Rhinewalt have pleaded not guilty to the criminal charge.

In his opening statement to the jury, Special Assistant Attorney General Luke Williamson said Lewis’ death was “not a justified killing. It was not self-defense. We will ask that you find the defendants guilty of manslaughter.”

Defense lawyer Merrida Coxwell Jr. told the jury of nine Black and three white members that officers blocked Lewis in with their car and called on him to show his hands. “Suddenly and without warning, Jaylen Lewis slammed into the back of the police car behind and came right at the officers,” he said.

In response to the 707-horsepower engine Cherokee heading toward them, Coxwell said Rhinewalt shot Lewis in self-defense. The earlier indictment concluded that was “not a reasonable belief under the circumstances.”

At the time of the fatal shooting, Frederick and Rhinewalt were conducting a narcotics operation when they saw a white Jeep Grand Cherokee turn north on West Street in Jackson driven by Lewis, who had a female passenger.

After the officers saw the Cherokee run a red light at Stonewall Street, they turned on their police lights and pulled Lewis over and blocked him from going forward with his car.

Lewis wound up reversing his car and bumping into the police cruiser behind his vehicle. 

After this, Frederick and Rhinewalt opened fire into the Cherokee, fatally shooting Lewis in the head, according to the lawsuit. 

In Lewis’ car, officers found Glock pistols, an assault weapon and bags of marijuana, Coxwell said. “We’re not trying to paint a negative picture, but it’s the truth.”

Lewis decided to run “probably because of the drugs and weapons,” Coxwell said. “That’s never a safe thing to do with officers standing in front of you.”

Lt. Kevin Swinney of Capitol Police testified he was present when the shooting took place. He said he didn’t see where Frederick and Rhinewalt were standing when they fired their guns.

Asked if the officers had done anything that fell outside police practice, Swinney replied no. If they had, Gilbert asked, “you would have reported it, right?”

Swinney responded yes. “I ain’t going to jail for nobody.”

Capt. Dennis Weaver of the Mississippi Bureau of Investigation testified that the passenger in Lewis’ vehicle, Selena Hayes, told agents that she yelled out, “Stop, stop, stop” when Lewis tried to speed off.

Speaking of Frederick, Coxwell asked Weaver: “As best you could tell, he was telling the truth?”

Weaver replied yes.

Ty Parker, crime scene analyst for MBI, identified two bullet holes in the front windshield of Lewis’ car and another two bullet holes on the driver’s side window.

She testified there was no sign that any of the weapons inside Lewis’ car were fired. All three guns were loaded, she said.

Just before the shooting, Chauncey Webster, a Capitol Police officer who was riding with Swinney, said the Cherokee “backed into us hard,” and he heard gunfire ring out.

Asked where Frederick and Rhinewalt were standing, he replied, “I wasn’t focused on that. I was trying not to get shot.”

The trial resumes Thursday.

In 2022, the state Legislature expanded the jurisdiction of Capitol Police beyond the Capitol and other government buildings in downtown Jackson. Within that year, officers shot at least four people.

A month before Lewis was killed, Rhinewalt and former Flex Unit officer Jeffery Walker opened fire on a car, striking a passenger in the head. That victim, Sherita Harris, survived but now has “permanent neurological and facial injuries,” according to her lawsuit.

A grand jury indicted Rhinewalt and Walker for aggravated assault in that case. According to a lawsuit filed against them in the case, no weapon was recovered from the car.

In March 2023, Frederick totaled his Capitol Police Ford vehicle, and flunked the DUI field test with a 0.15 score, nearly twice the legal limit of 0.8. Five months later he dodged conviction when a state trooper failed to appear for the court hearing. The judge dismissed the DUI charge.

Frederick resigned three days after the wreck “to prevent termination,” according to his certification records. A year and a half after the incident he wrecked another patrol vehicle, this time as a deputy for Scott County.

“Jaylen does not brandish a weapon, reach for a weapon, make any violent gestures, threaten anyone, or take any other actions that could be reasonably perceived as endangering officers or others,” according to a lawsuit filed by Lewis’ mother, Arkela Lewis.

U.S. District Judge Kristi H. Johnson has dismissed the Mississippi Department of Public Safety from the lawsuit, which remains pending against the former officers. Frederick and Rhinewalt have asked for it  to be dismissed.

In an interview outside the courthouse, Arkela Lewis said hearing all the justifications for killing her son angers her. Any time an officer kills someone, “It’s always self-defense,” she said. “It’s something I have already been prepared for.”

She said she is far from optimistic the officers will be convicted. “I’ve been praying and leaving it in God’s hands. That’s all I can do.”

Update, 9/23/2026: This story has been updated with additional details about the trial.

item.title: Opponent alleges US Rep. Ezell violated campaign finance laws. Ezell camp calls it a ‘political stunt’
item.dc:creator: Taylor Vance
item.description: The complaint focuses on the Chouest family, which owns shipbuilding company Edison Chouest Offshore. Family members donated to Ezell, who chairs the Subcommittee on Coast Guard and Maritime Transportation. Congress awarded the company a $950-million contract.
item.content:encoded:
Carl Boyanton, an independent candidate running for the 4th Congressional District, filed a complaint with the Federal Election Commission alleging his Republican opponent, U.S. Rep. Mike Ezell, accepted more money from campaign donors than the law allows. 

Boyanton, a business owner, filed the report against Ezell in June and focuses on seven members of the Chouest family, which owns shipbuilding company Edison Chouest Offshore. They donated to Ezell, who chairs the Subcommittee on Coast Guard and Maritime Transportation. The federal government eventually awarded the company a $950 million contract.  

“This is a classic pay-to-play scheme where special interests and billionaires think they can buy a Mississippi Congressman,” Boyanton said in a statement. “South Mississippians deserve a representative who answers to them, not to wealthy campaign donors or defense contractors seeking special favors.”

Josh Gregory, Ezell’s campaign manager, said in a statement that the campaign complies with federal campaign finance law. 

“While Mr. Boyanton’s allegations are obviously a political stunt, making a false statement to a federal agency, such as the FEC, is illegal and we will be reporting him for doing that,” Gregory said. “In the meantime, voters will have their say when they defeat him for the fourth time on November 3.”

The complaint centers on a joint fundraising committee called the Ezell Victory Fund, which Ezell’s campaign formed with the National Republican Congressional Committee and his leadership PAC, New Sheriff PAC.

The complaint alleges that seven members of the Chouest family, in August 2025, each gave $3,500 to Ezell’s primary campaign and $3,500 to his general election campaign, maxing out the $7,000-per-cycle limit an individual can give directly to a candidate, totaling $49,000. 

The family also donated another $150,000 to the joint fundraising committee: $10,000 each from five family members and $50,000 each from Gary and Carolyn Chouest.

The complaint argues that when the Ezell Victory Fund later transferred $47,625 of that money to Ezell’s campaign committee on Sept. 18, 2025, it amounted to funneling additional Chouest family money to the campaign beyond federal limits. 

But it’s unclear if what Boyanton is alleging actually took place because FEC records don’t typically show a donor-by-donor breakdown when a joint fundraising committee transfers a lump sum into a candidate’s personal fundraising committee. 

Federal rules require a joint fundraising committee to divide each donor’s contribution among its participating committees so that no individual’s total contribution to any one committee, whether given directly or through a joint account, exceeds that donor’s limit for that committee.

Even if Ezell violated the law, he is unlikely to face penalties anytime soon because the FEC, which is supposed to regulate campaign finances, doesn’t even have enough confirmed members to meet, let alone consider complaints, according to a recent report from the New York Times. 

Boyanton also alleges that the contractor and Ezell broke the law because contractors who receive money from Congress are prohibited from directly donating money to candidates and committees. 

But federal law does not prohibit individuals who have an ownership stake in a contractor company from making individual donations. 

Ezell, Boyanton and Democratic nominee Jeffrey Hulum will compete against each other during the general election on Nov. 3.
